description: A small evergreen, semi-parasitic tree 4-9 m tall with opposite thin lanceolate leaves, small reddish-purple flowers in panicles and round black fruits. The fragrant heartwood and its oil are prized.
cultural_significance: Chandana paste is used for tilak and in temple rituals, and the fragrance is central in Indian worship. Sandalwood is prominent in the epics and Nighantus. Not a Vedic-era plant by name with certainty. Karnataka has historically been the centre of the trade.
habitat: Dry deciduous forests of southern India (Karnataka and Tamil Nadu); a root hemi-parasite that needs host plants; now grown in plantations.

uses.title: Cooling skin paste
uses.detail: Chandana paste with rose water is traditionally applied on the forehead and skin to relieve heat, burning sensation, rashes and sunburn; described as Daha-prashamana.

uses.title: Acne and blemishes
uses.detail: Described as Varnya (improves complexion) and used in face packs for acne and pigmentation.

uses.title: Urinary burning and fever
uses.detail: A cold infusion of the wood is traditionally given for burning urination and heat-type fevers.

uses.title: Aromatherapy and calming
uses.detail: Sandalwood oil is used in aromatherapy and rituals for its calming scent; evidence is preliminary.

classical_refs: Charaka Samhita - listed among Dahaprashamana and Varnya herbs

preparations.name: Chandana lepa (paste)
preparations.method: Rub the wood on a wet stone to make a paste, optionally with rose water, and apply externally.

preparations.name: Chandana churna
preparations.method: Fine wood powder mixed with water, honey or milk.

preparations.name: Cold infusion (hima)
preparations.method: Soak powdered heartwood in water overnight and strain.

preparations.name: Sandalwood oil
preparations.method: Steam-distilled essential oil from heartwood; dilute before applying.
preparations.note: Costly and often adulterated; external or aroma use.

precautions: Essential oil can cause skin irritation or allergy and must be diluted and patch-tested; do not swallow the oil. Avoid internal medicinal use in pregnancy or kidney disease without guidance. The species is a regulated, protected tree in India, so wood must be legally sourced, and much market oil is adulterated.

cultivation.soil: Well-drained red loam; needs a host plant (e.g. Casuarina or pigeon pea) for roots
cultivation.propagation: Seeds with host plants; takes 15-30 years for fragrant heartwood
cultivation.harvest: Heartwood develops oil after many years; felling is regulated

conservation_status: Vulnerable (IUCN) due to over-harvesting and illegal felling.
fun_fact: Sandalwood is a root hemi-parasite: it taps the roots of neighbouring host trees for water and minerals, and the heartwood oil takes decades to form.

regions.name: Deccan Plateau
regions.note: Karnataka and Mysore plateau, the heartland of Indian sandalwood

regions.name: Tamil Nadu Plains
regions.note: Dry forests such as Javadi hills and Sathyamangalam

regions.name: Western Ghats
regions.note: Native on the dry eastern slopes

regions.name: Indonesia (Java, Sumatra & Maluku)
regions.note: Natural to the lesser Sunda islands; limited wild stands

regions.name: Northern Australia
regions.note: Commercial plantations in the Kimberley region
